To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

3-nitropionic acid (N-PA), a mitochondrial complex II inhibitor, induces a highly reproducible pattern of brain damage in rats that is similar in many ways to hypoxic brain injury from other causes including hypoglycemic coma and ischemia.
subcutaneous injection with 3-nitrpropionic acid (3-NPA) produces histotoxic hypoxiain the brain of rats that are in the recumbent position.

3-nitropopionic acid (3-NP) intoxication in rats produces a selective, bilaterially symmetrical pattern of brain damage that is similar to that seen following hypoglycemic coma in man and animals, and that is characterized by selective neuronal injury in the caudoventral caudate nucleus and putamen (caudate-putaminal complex).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the brain damage induced by 3-NP in rats.
the development of a new model of brain injury in rats.
the development of a model of brain injury that is characterized by selective neuronal and white matter injury, and is associated with the development of clinical signs of neurological disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain lesions of NPA intoxication are consistent with the concept of histotoxic hypoxemia (energy deficient hypoxia) rather than hypoxemia per se.
3-nitropionic acid-induced brain lesions are a type of hypoxic brain damage.

NPA intoxication produces a pattern of morphological brain damage similar to that seen in human and experimental hypoxic brain injury, and that NPA intoxicates rats are a valid animal model of hypoxic brain injury.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NPA model of brain injury is a useful model for hypoxia, and is different than other models of brain injury.

NPA intoxication in rats is a model of hypoxic brain damage with a unique pattern of brain lesions, and that the pattern of brain damage is not a consequence of the pattern of blood flow, but rather a consequence of the energy deficiency induced by NPA.

3-nitropionic acid (3-NPA) intoxication produces brain injury that is highly specific in its anatomical distribution and that is consistent with the concept of a hypoxic (energy-deficient) brain injury.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain lesions in rats intoxicated with NPA are very different from the brain lesions in the other animal models of hypoxia.
NPA intoxication is a model of energy-deficiency-induced brain damage, which is distinct from ischemic or hypoglycemic brain damage.
the NPA rat model of hypoxic (or energy deficient) brain damage can be used to investigate mechanisms of brain damage in a variety of disease states.
